title: Thoreau's limits
hookLine: critics call him prickly and self-righteous, and his friends sometimes agreed

cards: After Thoreau died, Emerson, his friend, wrote a long tribute to him.
And right in the middle of the praise, he slips in a sentence that sounds almost like a complaint: "It cost him nothing to say No; indeed he found it much easier than to say Yes."
That's a friend talking, not an enemy, in a tribute meant to honor him. After weeks of Thoreau's best lines, today, honestly, the other side.

teach.b: First, the no. Refusal came easily to Thoreau. It's the same quality that sent him to jail rather than pay a tax he found unjust, and the one that could make him hard to be around.

teach.h: THE ARM OF AN ELM TREE.
teach.b: Second, the elm tree. Emerson passes on a friend's line: I love Henry, "but I cannot like him; and as for taking his arm, I should as soon think of taking the arm of an elm-tree." Love, yes.
Ease, no. Upright, rooted, and not soft to lean on. Third, the huckleberry party.
Emerson counts it a fault that Thoreau had no ambition.
He thought Thoreau had the gifts to lead great public work, and instead, he writes, "Instead of engineering for all America, he was the captain of a huckleberry-party."
Some hear a put-down; others hear quiet praise in it: he chose to lead friends to the berries. Fourth, the critics.
Some readers since have found Thoreau preachy, scornful of his neighbors, quick to judge how others lived while he lived so differently. Those are fair things to notice; his books do scold.
But see what Emerson does: he names the prickles, then keeps praising. The tribute holds both.
A person can be hard to like and still be good, and still be worth learning from. That may be what Thoreau's friends teach best about him.

how: Some readers of Thoreau hold his sharpness and his goodness together, much as Emerson did in his tribute, naming the prickles without throwing out the man.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is hard to like: not someone who harms you, just someone sharp, stubborn, quick to say no. Name one prickle honestly, then, like Emerson, name one real good thing in them.
Hold both at once, love without pretending it's easy.
